title: Topological Quantum Interferometry
authors: Tianyou Ying, Yufeng Zhou, Chengwei Pan, Ryan Hogan, Ruoyang Zhang, Hui Liu, Shining Zhu, Xiaoqin Gao
abstract: Structured light provides high-dimensional Hilbert spaces holding tremendous potential for fundamental quantum optics and quantum technologies. However, existing characterization methods, like Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference, typically assume perfectly tuned conditions, overlooking the geometric physics governing spatial mode evolution. Here, we establish topological quantum interferometry driven by an interaction-based geometric phase, the exchange Berry phase (BPX). Our formalism generalizes $q$-plate state generation and characterization to arbitrary topological charges and (de)tuning conditions, demonstrating that BPX acts as a geometric marker governing spatial interference. We show BPX serves as a deterministic control parameter, decomposing two-photon spatial patterns into geometry-dictated fundamental modes. This mapping reveals topological invariants and phase singularities that function as a non-tomographic witness for state dimensionality estimation, circumventing full-state reconstruction. Being device-independent and highly scalable, this approach enables scalable high-dimensional characterization and topologically protected state selection, with direct applicability to quantum metrology and high-capacity quantum networks.
summary: The paper introduces topological quantum interferometry using the exchange Berry phase (BPX) to characterize high-dimensional quantum states generated by structured light. It shows that the resulting spatial interference patterns contain topological invariants that can non-tomographically estimate the state's dimensionality. This offers a scalable and robust method for quantum metrology and network applications.
main_problem: The core problem is developing methods to characterize high-dimensional quantum states using topological principles, overcoming limitations of traditional characterization techniques that assume ideal experimental conditions.
main_result: The exchange Berry phase (BPX) acts as a deterministic control parameter whose associated phase singularities serve as a non-tomographic witness for estimating the state's dimensionality.
method: The authors establish a formalism based on topological quantum interferometry, generalizing $q$-plate state generation and characterization to arbitrary detuning conditions. They calculate Bell state probabilities and visibility using geometric phases derived from the BPX.
model_or_system: The system involves structured light interacting via two-photon interference at a beamsplitter, utilizing q-plates whose action is described by unitary transformations involving topological charges ($q$) and detunings ($\delta$).

main_assumptions: The analysis relies on decomposing the state into fundamental modes governed by geometry, and some calculations simplify the radial dependence of the field components.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the conceptual framework of interference patterns dictated by BPX, show phase evolution across Bell basis states under varying detuning/charge, and map out spatial probability distributions for different input polarizations.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the physical model (q-plates and structured light) to deriving the mathematical formalism using geometric phases ($	ext{BPX}$). It then applies this framework to calculate observable quantities like Bell state probabilities and visibility, culminating in demonstrating how topological invariants provide a dimensionality witness.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, device-independent tool for characterizing complex quantum states (high-dimensional entanglement) using purely geometric principles derived from interference patterns, which is highly relevant for scalable quantum network characterization.
